analysis.one_liner: Lets unions negotiate contracts requiring workers to pay union fees, even in states that currently ban it.
analysis.headline: Introduced in late September 2010 with 17 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to committee and then to a subcommittee, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2011 without any hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, about half of U.S. states have "right to work" laws that bar union contracts requiring workers to join or pay a union as a condition of keeping their job. This bill would erase that state option by repealing the federal provision (Section 14(b) of the Labor-Management Relations Act) that allows states to ban such agreements. After repeal, unions could negotiate contracts requiring union membership or fees in every state, including ones where voters' state law currently forbids it. The bill was introduced two months before the end of the two-year session, got a committee referral and then a subcommittee referral, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Union members and unions in right-to-work states benefit most: unions gain the ability to negotiate contracts requiring union membership or fees, which adds dues-paying members and revenue. Workers covered by union contracts who would otherwise ride free on union representation would be asked to contribute. Workers in states without right-to-work laws see no change.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Section 14(b) of the Labor-Management Relations Act, the provision that lets states ban union-security agreements; after repeal, a union contract requiring union membership or fees as a condition of employment would be enforceable in every state.
This ends the situation where a union must represent workers in right-to-work states who cannot be required to pay for that representation, letting those workers be asked to share the cost.
The change would apply nationwide, preempting contrary state or territorial law.

analysis.who_pays: Workers in right-to-work states who do not want to belong to a union would bear the cost, since union contracts could require them to pay union fees to keep their jobs. Employers in those states would face union security provisions they are currently shielded from.

drawbacks.text: The bill would override right-to-work laws in the states that have them, meaning a worker in those states who does not want to join or support a union could be required to pay union fees as a condition of employment under a union-negotiated contract.

Under existing federal law, workers subject to a union-security agreement can only be charged an agency fee covering bargaining costs rather than full membership dues; the bill would open the door to broader mandatory-fee arrangements in every state, a change that costs money for workers who prefer not to belong.

The bill removes a state-law protection by amending federal statute, raising the standard objection that employment rules of this kind should remain a matter of state choice rather than a single national rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is real for union-covered workers in right-to-work states: dues-paying members stop subsidizing free-riding coworkers, and unions get more resources to bargain. The cost is borne by workers who do not want to belong: roughly half the country's states would no longer be able to guarantee them the choice, and they could face required union fees as a condition of keeping their job. The bill was also a blunt instrument — it simply erased Section 14(b) rather than crafting any accommodation, such as limiting fees to bargaining costs — and it was introduced too late in the session, with minimal support, to have a realistic path.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and Labor Committee and then in a subcommittee, was never given a hearing or a vote, and expired when the two-year Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor on the day it was introduced, September 29, 2010, and was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions on November 18, 2010.
The action history shows no further steps — no committee markup, no report to the House, and no floor vote — through the end of the 111th Congress.
The bill page for H.R. 6384 in the 111th Congress records no final action; the Congress ended January 3, 2011, and all bills not enacted by then died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in right-to-work states and the anti-union-fee status quo came out ahead: no worker in those states can now be required to support a union, and unions gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Right-to-work employers and the status quo

for.name: Rep. Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 29, 2010 to repeal the federal provision letting states ban union-security agreements.

for.name: 17 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: George Miller
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to and never brought it up for a hearing or markup; it died there at the end of the session.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and it died in committee without a recorded vote.

industries.note: Unions would gain a nationwide right to negotiate union-security agreements, adding members and fee revenue in the roughly half of states that currently bar it. More union revenue also means more resources for bargaining on behalf of covered workers.

Employers operating in states that prohibit mandatory union membership would lose the protection those state laws provide, and union contracts covering their workers could require fees. Their current ability to run union-free or fee-free workplaces would end where a majority of employees vote for a union.

Workers covered by a union contract in right-to-work states could be required to pay union fees as a condition of employment, ending their current ability to work there without paying. This is a direct cost to them, though federal law limits such fees to bargaining-related costs rather than full political dues.
